Xutang Zhiyu, Tiantong Rujing, and Baiyun Shouduan extend the same official-sounding submission formula to live mechanisms, failed public responses, and the assembly's seeing. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1390.xml). Expanded Record of Chan Master Xisou Shaotan. Xisou Shaotan gives the pair during a winter-night address amid his ridicule of hall notices, ghost-faced hexagrams and fruit tables. Immediately after the seasonal formula he asks why one should meddle in those affairs, then calls the obstructing objects four pieces of wood that have twisted people's noses through the ages. He says he will cut them apart and asks who can distinguish fragrance from stench. Those who can are compared with a wild plum blooming before the full cold; those who cannot are warned not to swallow a date whole while eating fruit. The decline of the petty and growth of the noble is therefore something he challenges the assembly to handle, not simply a forecast that deserving people will prosper. The headword is rendered: The way of the petty wanes; the way of the noble waxes.

He asks what one could say about all yin being stripped away and one yang returning before the undivided cosmos has separated at all, and follows with the question of what talk of the petty waning and noble growing could mean there. His later account of forces generating and overcoming one another leads into criticism of earlier teachers' elaborate handling. He challenges the assembly for a phrase before that separation, then says that even a completely successful saying is still a matter of left and right. Senses.Explanation: The way of the petty wanes; the way of the noble waxes. Xisou Shaotan gives the pair during a winter-night address amid his ridicule of hall notices, ghost-faced hexagrams and fruit tables. Immediately after the seasonal formula he asks why one should meddle in those affairs, then calls the obstructing objects four pieces of wood that have twisted people's noses through the ages. He says he will cut them apart and asks who can distinguish fragrance from stench. Those who can are compared with a wild plum blooming before the full cold; those who cannot are warned not to swallow a date whole while eating fruit. The decline of the petty and growth of the noble is therefore something he challenges the assembly to handle, not simply a forecast that deserving people will prosper. Senses.Explanation: A courtesy formula of unexpected gain — went out small and met great — supplied at the root by Yunmen for a speechless newcomer, and claimed, graded, denied, staged, and promised across the Song case-halls and the Qing assemblies. The root sits in Yunmen Wenyan's own screening-talk record: a newcomer is asked — on South Peak you borrowed two hundred coins of me; why do you not repay? — and at his silence the master lends him the answer: today I went out small and met great; and again: today the occasion passed me by; Xutang Zhiyu's hall carries the courtesy line live — not only did the great assembly behold the sight; I went out small and met great — and the grading answer lands at once: a thieving-mind little devil; the monk bows, the master raises his staff: were it me, Huqiu come directly down, like a rich heir of many generations not one coin misspent, each life fierce and cramped only because the family discipline is too strict; Dachuan Puji raises Huitang Zuxin's Nanxiong monk — better go home; in your village three coins buy a piece of fish-roe palm-sized — and rules: rather be ground to dust than blind one monk's eyes; Huitang's cooked place unforgotten, but that monk did not know going-out-small-meeting-great — had he known to raise fist and spirit, where in the world was there room for him?; and Shitian Faxun, over the emperor's cloud-rest hermit who came wordless to court with Xuedou's supplied answer — none escapes the perfect transforming — finds Xuedou true to the coming occasion yet still a shrimp that cannot leap out: were I the new abbot, I would have answered then: today I went out small and met great — does it still meet the sagely intent? a long stillness, then: used to passing before the five-phoenix tower, hand on the golden whip, hailing the great peace. Shending Yikui raises the scholar with the Thousand-Buddha Name Sutra — a hundred thousand buddhas seen by name only, what land do they dwell in, do they convert beings? — and Changsha Jingcen's return: since Cui Hao inscribed the poem on Yellow Crane Tower, has the scholar inscribed one? not yet — then find leisure to set down a good one; Yikui rules the old great teacher well met the coming impulse, yet imposed on another what he himself would not wish; the scholar went out small and met great, how it outdoes the airs — and yet his nostrils remain in another man's hands; setting that aside: does the assembly want to know the going-out-small-meeting-great affair? without the connoisseur's eye of Zhonglang, it is still firewood at a rustic shed; Yuan'an Liao, in an address of praise where the buddhas cannot speak it, the founding teachers cannot lift it, the ten great commentators cannot annotate it, the world's patch-robed ones cannot reach it — heaven and earth not vast enough, sun and moon not bright enough, the hungry fed and the sick righted — widens the promise past all courtesy: making everyone come empty and return full, setting each and all to go out small and meet great, the three wretched roads turned to level highways and the six desires' turning wheel stilled; and Yushan Shangsi, at the birthday seat his senior monks and the mountain elders beg him to take, hears the claim from the asking monk — today I too go out small and meet great — and turns it back: what is the affair of your meeting? the monk answers with the hero's line — to stand out from the herd one must be a bold spirit; to win the field, a lion's cub — and the master checks the boasting: a fine hand, over-praised.

Senses.Explanation: A “small convocation” is a named communal address, often held in the evening or for a special occasion, whose procedure and content are less fixed than an ordinary hall address. The Baizhang rules say it has no fixed location, may use the sleeping hall or teaching hall according to attendance, is announced by a placard, omits the release-from-consultation bell, gathers the community after the evening bell, and lets the resident master mount the seat. The same rules list occasions including installation, visiting officials or donors, special requests, instruction for the dead, and seasonal observances. Records then mark small convocations for year-end, opening or closing a retreat, memorial instruction, ordination, and ordinary evening teaching. A playful interview answers “what is a small convocation?” with “eating gruel,” contrasting a great convocation with eating rice. These uses identify an event format, not a diminutive teaching.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J29/J29nB222.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zishui of Wolong, Kuizhou. Zishui voices the inherited comparison of lesser and greater knowledge and years, then stages Zhuangzi displaying his skill at the Zhiyue gate. Pillars and lamps turn him about until he has eyes without seeing and ears without hearing, and he returns seeking a saying. Zishui answers that when clever devices are exhausted, thoughts are exhausted, and when white clouds disperse, green mountains appear. The opening hierarchy is subjected to this imagined teaching test; the current speaker is Zishui, not a historical Zhuangzi visiting the monastery.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB191.xml). Xiangtian Jinian Sayings. Jinian Jingxian asks why no one can take up what he presents like a king's jewel given with both hands. Among several possible obstructions he asks whether narrow views and mistrustful doubt make haste turn into delay. He repeats the headword while answering each possible obstruction: if this is the trouble, why not let it be natural, with no fixed coming or staying? Other obstacles call for other responses, and he finally asks someone to complete his unfinished instruction, without accepting the listeners' answers. The saying is his current application, not a diagnosis that every listener has precisely the same fault or a general excuse for intermittent practice.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J33/J33nB280.xml). Shending Yunwaize Sayings. Yunwai Xingze surveys mistaken approaches to practice. One group alternates between doubt and trust, effort and negligence, yet boasts that inquiry now continues without being deliberately raised and wonders why great awakening has not come. He calls this narrow vision and mistrustful doubt making haste slower, and asks how genuine sustained doubt could work where there is no settled commitment. Senses.Explanation: To leak out or show through. Chan records most often use the expression as a retrospective appraisal after someone has spoken or acted: 'it leaked out,' 'quite a lot leaked out,' 'the whole body leaked out,' or 'one could not avoid leaking once.' Foyan applies the same verdict in succession to Deshan's statement that his house has no phrases and no single thing to give people, Xuefeng's statement that he went empty-handed and returned empty-handed, and Muzhou's calling an unnamed monk a board-carrying fellow. The Blue Cliff Record says that much had leaked out when Bodhidharma pressed Emperor Wu at the outset. A later direct question, 'What is the place of leaking out?' receives a list of recorded expressions and objects: Yunmen's flatbread, Zhaozhou's tea, Xuefeng's wooden ball, and Zihu's dog. The records do not identify a single substance that leaks, and this entry adds none.

Senses.Explanation: A golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net figures an exceptional adept no longer caught by ordinary devices. The phrase is anchored in Sansheng’s public question to Xuefeng: “What does the golden-scaled fish through the net feed on?” (透網金鱗未審以何為食); Xuefeng replies that he will tell him after he comes out of the net. Yuanwu’s prose supplies the corpus’s direct definition: “only with an eye at the crown is one called a golden-scaled fish through the net” (頂門有眼方謂之透網金鱗). The image then becomes an appraisal of monks: Baowen Hongyin hails a patch-robed monastic as “excellent—a patch-robed monk, a golden-scaled fish through the net” (俊哉衲子，透網金鱗), while later interviews ask why such a fish is still held up by water.

Senses.Explanation: To pass the barrier is to get through a tested obstruction: the records contrast those already through with those still stopped, and extend the phrase to a barrier-passing eye and phrase. Huanglong Huinan distinguishes the two conditions: 'one already past the barrier swings his arms and goes straight on' (已過關者掉臂徑去), whereas 'this is one who has not passed the barrier' (此未透關者也). Zhongfeng Mingben records a corrective contrast: people thread all old and new public cases onto one string and call it 'passing the barrier' (謂之透關), while 'the tight barrier of life and death beneath their heels has not actually been passed' (脚跟下一座生死牢關。政好不曾透得。). The phrase also builds 'an eye that passes the barrier' (透關眼). Yuanwu Keqin asks whether anyone present has such an eye. Chijue Daochong says, 'Passing the barrier requires a barrier-passing eye; obtaining treasure requires one who can distinguish treasure' (透關須具透關眼，得寶須還別寶人). Poshan Haiming answers the question 'What is a phrase that passes the barrier?' (如何是透關句), and Dabian Xianquan contrasts 'one already through the barrier' (已透關者) with 'one not through the barrier' (未透關者). These are recorded descriptions, corrections, and compounds; this entry adds no unrecorded destination beyond the barrier.

Senses.Explanation: An eye that sees through the barrier is the capacity Chan records demand for distinguishing speakers, cases, and what lies beyond a named barrier. Yunju Zhuang says those who teach must possess this eye to distinguish false from correct and recognize the arriving situation. Yuanwu Keqin and other hall speakers publicly ask whether anyone with such an eye will come forward. Ying'an Tanhua says lineage teachers lacking it cannot distinguish the black from the white when extending a hand. Xutang Zhiyu calls someone who grasps only an immediately available statement a person who has not yet acquired this eye.
